The arrival of the craft of papermaking in Samarkand, in Central Asia, in the mid 8th century, the first step in its spread from China to the Islamic world and Europe.

Paper was invented in China. Court official Cai Lun is credited with improving it in 105 CE, and for centuries the Chinese kept the craft largely to themselves. Paper had travelled west along the trade routes as a good, but not the skill to make it.

The traditional story ties the transfer to the Battle of Talas in 751, where Abbasid forces beat a Tang army near the Talas River. Chinese prisoners taken there, the story says, included papermakers who taught the craft in Samarkand. Historians doubt the details; paper may already have been made in Central Asia by then, through Sogdian traders or Buddhist monasteries. Still, from around this time Samarkand paper became famous.

How it spread from there:

  • To Baghdad by the late 8th century, where the Abbasid bureaucracy adopted it for records.
  • To Damascus, Cairo and North Africa over the next centuries.
  • To Muslim Spain by the 11th century and then to Christian Europe, with mills in Italy by the late 13th century.

Cheap paper made books, records and letters far easier to produce. It fed the great age of Arabic learning in Baghdad, and centuries later the printing press of Johannes Gutenberg in Europe depended on it.
sum: The arrival of the craft of papermaking in Samarkand, in Central Asia, in the mid 8th century, the first step in its spread from China to the Islamic world and Europe.
